questions.name: fstab — the six fields
questions.task: You need the field layout of /etc/fstab. Type the command that opens the right page.
questions.explain: fstab(5) is the file format. mount(8) is the command. Plain `man fstab` happens to land on 5 here because nothing else claims the name, but typing the number is the habit that saves you when a name lives in two sections.
questions.mnemonic: Five letters in F-I-E-L-D. If you edit the file, read 5.

questions.name: admin commands
questions.task: useradd, mount, lvextend and vgcreate all share one man section. Type its number.
questions.explain: Section 8 is system administration commands — the ones that normally need root. Almost every LFCS task verb lives here.
questions.mnemonic: 8 looks like a padlock stacked twice. Locked = root only.

questions.name: crontab — the five time fields
questions.task: You have forgotten the order of the five cron time fields. Type the command that shows them.
questions.explain: crontab(1) documents the *command* — how to edit and list. crontab(5) documents the *file* — the five fields, @reboot, ranges and steps. Bare `man crontab` gives you 1 and leaves you no wiser.
questions.mnemonic: Five fields, section five.

questions.name: chage — the section trap
questions.task: Password aging with chage. Type the section number its page lives in.
questions.explain: chage is section 1, not 8, even though it reads like an admin tool — because an unprivileged user may run `chage -l` on their own account. useradd, usermod and userdel are 8; chage, passwd and gpasswd are 1.
questions.mnemonic: You can chage yourself, so it is a user command. Self-service means section 1.

questions.name: passwd — the seven fields
questions.task: You need the colon-separated field layout of /etc/passwd, not the command that changes passwords. Type it.
questions.explain: passwd(1) changes a password. passwd(5) describes the file. This is the cleanest example of why the number matters — the same name, two entirely different pages, and bare `man passwd` gives you the wrong one.
questions.mnemonic: Same word, two jobs. 1 does it, 5 describes it.

questions.name: read every match
questions.task: Show every man page named passwd, one after another, section 1 then section 5. Type the command.
questions.explain: -a walks all matches instead of stopping at the lowest-numbered one. Quit one page with q and the next opens. Useful when you know the name but not which section holds the thing you want.
questions.mnemonic: -a for all the way through.

questions.name: sysctl — three sections deep
questions.task: sysctl exists in 2 (the syscall), 5 (sysctl.conf) and 8 (the command). Open the page for the command you run at a shell.
questions.explain: sysctl(8) documents -w, -p, -a and --system. sysctl.conf(5) documents the file syntax. sysctl(2) is the C system call and is no use to you on this exam.
questions.mnemonic: Run it at a prompt with sudo, look in 8.

questions.name: sysctl.d drop-ins
questions.task: A task wants a kernel parameter to survive reboot via a drop-in file. You need the naming and precedence rules for /etc/sysctl.d/. Type the command.
questions.explain: sysctl.d(5) is where the .conf suffix requirement, the numeric-prefix ordering, and the /etc over /usr/lib precedence are written down. This page answers more Operations Deployment questions than sysctl(8) does.
questions.mnemonic: Any /etc/*.d directory has its own section 5 page named after the directory.

questions.name: the filesystem layout
questions.task: You want the reference for what belongs in /srv vs /var vs /usr/share. Type the command.
questions.explain: hier(7) is the filesystem hierarchy overview. Section 7 holds conventions and overviews rather than commands or file formats.
questions.mnemonic: hier as in hierarchy. Overviews live in 7.

questions.name: device files
questions.task: Type the section number that documents special files under /dev, such as loop and null.
questions.explain: Section 4 is devices and special files. You rarely need it on LFCS, but knowing it exists stops you hunting through 5 and 8 for loop(4).
questions.mnemonic: 1 user, 2 syscall, 3 library, 4 device, 5 file format, 6 games, 7 overview, 8 admin.

questions.name: sudoers, two pages
questions.task: You need the sudoers file syntax, and separately the tool that edits it safely. Type both commands.
questions.explain: sudoers(5) carries the user-host-runas grammar and the NOPASSWD tag. visudo(8) carries -c for a syntax check and -f for an alternate file. Two pages, two jobs.
questions.mnemonic: Grammar in 5, the editor that enforces it in 8.

questions.name: timer units
questions.task: You are writing a .timer unit and need OnBootSec, Persistent and Unit. Type the command.
questions.explain: Every systemd unit type has its own section 5 page: systemd.unit, systemd.service, systemd.timer, systemd.mount, systemd.socket. The directives for [Timer] are only in systemd.timer(5).
questions.mnemonic: Unit files are files, so they are section 5, one page per unit type.

questions.name: the directive you cannot find
questions.task: You need User=, Environment= and WorkingDirectory= for a service unit, and they are not in systemd.service(5). Type the page that has them.
questions.explain: systemd.service(5) documents Type=, ExecStart= and Restart=. Everything about the execution environment — user, group, environment, working directory, sandboxing — was factored out into systemd.exec(5) because [Service], [Socket] and [Mount] all share it.
questions.mnemonic: How it runs is in .service. What it runs as is in .exec.

questions.name: resource limits
questions.task: A task asks you to raise nofile for a user in /etc/security/limits.conf. Type the command for the syntax.
questions.explain: limits.conf(5) has the four-column domain/type/item/value table and the full item list. pam_limits(8) is the module that reads it — a different page, and not the one with the syntax.
questions.mnemonic: The file has a section 5 page named exactly like the file.

questions.name: sshd keywords
questions.task: You need PermitRootLogin, AllowUsers and the Match block syntax. Type the command.
questions.explain: sshd_config(5) is the server keyword list. ssh_config(5) is the client one, and mixing them up costs you the task. sshd(8) is the daemon itself.
questions.mnemonic: The d is for daemon. sshd_config for the server, ssh_config for you.

questions.name: NFS mount options
questions.task: You are mounting an export and need vers=, soft, hard, timeo and retrans. Type the command.
questions.explain: nfs(5) is the mount option reference, and it is one of the highest-value pages on the whole exam. mount(8) points you here rather than repeating it.
questions.mnemonic: Mount options are read out of a file, so they are documented in 5.

questions.name: you do not know the command name
questions.task: You need something to do with disk quotas but cannot remember any command name. Type the command that searches page names and descriptions for quota.
questions.explain: man -k is apropos: it searches the one-line NAME descriptions of every page. It is the fastest way out of a blank on this exam, and it costs you about three seconds.
questions.mnemonic: -k for keyword. Do not know the name, know a word.

questions.name: nothing appropriate
questions.task: man -k returns "nothing appropriate" on a freshly built minimal box. Type the command that fixes it.
questions.explain: apropos and whatis read a prebuilt index, not the pages themselves. On a minimal install or a container that index does not exist yet. mandb builds it. Learn this now rather than discovering it under the clock.
questions.mnemonic: The db in mandb is the database that -k reads. No db, no keywords.

questions.name: the brute-force search
questions.task: You remember a directive called OnCalendar but not which page defines it. Type the command that searches the full text of every man page.
questions.explain: -K is global-apropos: it greps the body of every page, not just the descriptions. It is slow enough to hurt, so narrow it with a section when you can — man -K -s 5 OnCalendar. Capital K, and the difference from lowercase k is not cosmetic.
questions.mnemonic: Little k, little search — just the descriptions. Big K, big search — every word of every page.

questions.name: what does this thing do
questions.task: Print the one-line description of ss without opening the page. Type the command.
questions.explain: whatis is man -f: exact name lookup, one line back. It also reveals every section the name exists in, which is a quick way to spot a 1-and-5 collision before you open the wrong one.
questions.mnemonic: whatis asks what it is. apropos asks what is about this.

questions.name: narrow the search
questions.task: Search descriptions for mount but only inside section 5, so you get file formats rather than a screen of commands. Type the command.
questions.explain: -s takes a comma- or colon-separated section list and works on apropos, whatis and man alike. Pair it with -K when a full-text search would otherwise take a minute.
questions.mnemonic: -s for section, and it accepts a list: -s 5,8.

questions.name: too many hits
questions.task: apropos mount returns forty lines. Type the command that matches the keyword exactly instead of on word boundaries.
questions.explain: -e requires the keyword to match a whole page name or description rather than appearing inside one. It is the difference between four results and forty.
questions.mnemonic: -e for exact.

questions.name: both words, not either
questions.task: You want pages whose description mentions both nfs and mount, not either one. Type the command.
questions.explain: apropos defaults to OR across keywords. -a switches it to AND. Two keywords with -a will usually get you to the right page in one shot where one keyword gets you a wall.
questions.mnemonic: -a for and. -e for exact. Both are narrowing tools.

questions.name: where does the page live
questions.task: Print the path of the source file for the sshd_config page instead of displaying it. Type the command.
questions.explain: -w prints the location rather than rendering. Handy when you want to grep or zcat the raw page, or to confirm which of several installed copies you are actually reading.
questions.mnemonic: -w for where.

questions.name: anchor the keyword
questions.task: man -k treats the keyword as a regular expression. Type the search that matches only pages whose name starts with chage.
questions.explain: Because -k takes a regex, ^ and $ work. Anchoring turns a noisy search into a precise one without needing -e.
questions.mnemonic: It is a regex, so treat it like grep.

questions.name: where is man looking
questions.task: Print the list of directories man searches for pages. Type the command.
questions.explain: manpath shows the resolved search path. If a page you just installed is not being found, this is the first thing to check — and manpath(5) documents the config file behind it.
questions.mnemonic: Like PATH, but for pages.

questions.name: get to the examples
questions.task: You are inside a long man page. Type exactly what you press to jump to the EXAMPLES heading.
questions.explain: man renders through less, so every less search works. Headings are uppercase, so searching for the uppercase word lands on the heading rather than on prose mentions of the word.
questions.mnemonic: Headings shout. Search in caps to hit the heading, not the paragraph.

questions.name: repeat the search
questions.task: The first hit was not the one you wanted. Type the key for the next match, then the key for the previous match.
questions.explain: Lowercase n goes forward, uppercase N goes back. Same as vim, which is worth leaning on since you are drilling both.
questions.mnemonic: Shift reverses. Everywhere in less, and in vim too.

questions.name: both ends of the page
questions.task: Type the key that jumps to the end of the page, then the key that jumps back to the top.
questions.explain: g and G in less, same as vim's gg and G. Jumping to the end is how you check whether a page has an EXAMPLES or SEE ALSO section without scrolling through it.
questions.mnemonic: Big G goes to the big end.

questions.name: leave
questions.task: Type the key that closes the pager and returns you to the shell.
questions.explain: q quits. Worth being deliberate about because Ctrl+C does not close less, and on the exam a stuck pager wastes seconds you are counting.
questions.mnemonic: q for quit, and it is the same key in less, top and journalctl.

questions.name: hide everything else
questions.task: Inside mount(8) you want to see only the lines that mention noexec. Type exactly what you press.
questions.explain: & filters the display to matching lines only — the rest are hidden, not just skipped. On a page as long as mount(8) or nfs(5) this turns two minutes of scrolling into one line of typing. Press & then Enter with an empty pattern to switch it off.
questions.mnemonic: & is grep inside less. The one pager key most people never learn.

questions.name: search backwards
questions.task: You scrolled past the option you wanted. Type exactly what you press to search backwards for noexec.
questions.explain: / searches forward, ? searches backward. n and N then step through the results in whichever direction you started.
questions.mnemonic: Forward slash leans forward. The question mark curls back.

questions.name: the pager's own help
questions.task: You have forgotten a less key mid-page. Type the key that shows the full command summary.
questions.explain: h prints the complete less command list, inside the pager, offline. The less man page itself says that if you forget every other command, remember this one.
questions.mnemonic: h for help, and it is allowed in the exam because it is not the internet.

questions.name: half a screen
questions.task: Type the keystroke that scrolls down half a screen — finer than a full page when you are skimming an option list.
questions.explain: Ctrl-d is half a screen down, Ctrl-u is half a screen up, Space is a full screen. Half-screen scrolling keeps a few lines of context on screen, which matters when you are reading a table of mount options.
questions.mnemonic: d for down, u for up, and hold Ctrl for half.

questions.name: the other documentation tree
questions.task: man has nothing useful, but the package shipped a README and a sample config. Type the directory you look in.
questions.explain: Every packaged program may drop READMEs, changelogs and example configs under /usr/share/doc/<package>/. Your exam notes list it as an allowed reference alongside man, and it often holds a working sample config you can copy rather than write.
questions.mnemonic: hier(7) says it plainly: documentation about installed programs.

questions.name: what did this package install
questions.task: On a Debian-family host, list every file the nfs-common package installed. Type the command.
questions.explain: dpkg -L lists a package's files, which is how you find its docs, its unit files and its example configs when you do not know their paths.
questions.mnemonic: -L for list files. Capital L, because lowercase -l lists packages.

questions.name: just the documentation
questions.task: On an RPM host, list only the documentation files belonging to chrony. Type the command.
questions.explain: -qd queries doc files only, so you skip the binaries and libraries. -ql gives you everything, -qc gives you just the config files — that last one is worth remembering too.
questions.mnemonic: q query, then d docs, l list all, c config.

questions.name: three locations at once
questions.task: Find the binary, the source and the man page for nft in one command. Type it.
questions.explain: whereis returns binary, source and manual locations. which only returns the executable, and type tells you whether the shell would even reach a file.
questions.mnemonic: which is one answer, whereis is three.

questions.name: builtin or binary
questions.task: You want to know whether cd is a shell builtin, an alias or a file on disk. Type the command.
questions.explain: This matters because builtins have no man page of their own — they are documented inside bash(1). If type says builtin, stop looking for cd(1) and search inside man bash instead.
questions.mnemonic: If type says builtin, the docs are in bash(1), under SHELL BUILTIN COMMANDS.

questions.name: which package owns this file
questions.task: A config file exists and you want the package it came from. Type the RPM command, then the Debian one.
questions.explain: Once you have the package name, dpkg -L or rpm -qd gets you to its docs and examples. This is the two-step that turns an unfamiliar config file into a documented one.
questions.mnemonic: rpm asks -qf, which file. dpkg asks -S, search.

questions.name: the unit as loaded
questions.task: Print the unit file systemd is actually using for chronyd, including any drop-in overrides. Type the command.
questions.explain: systemctl cat prints the real file with its path, and appends every /etc/systemd/system/*.d/ drop-in in order. Faster than hunting the path yourself, and it shows you which overrides are live.
questions.mnemonic: cat the unit, not the file, and you get the overrides for free.

questions.name: every systemd directive
questions.task: You know the directive name but not which of the fifteen systemd pages defines it. Type the command that opens the master index.
questions.explain: systemd.directives(7) is an index of every directive systemd understands, each pointing at the page that documents it. There is also systemd.index(7) for page names. These two save more time than any other lookup on the systemd side.
questions.mnemonic: Lost in systemd? Ask the directives index which page owns the word.

questions.name: make it persist
questions.task: Task: set vm.swappiness to 10 and make it survive reboot. You have forgotten whether the drop-in file needs a .conf suffix. One command.
questions.explain: It does need .conf, and files are read in lexical order with /etc winning over /usr/lib. All of that is on one page. Going to sysctl(8) instead gives you the flags but not the file rules.
questions.mnemonic: The command is 8, the drop-in directory is 5.

questions.name: every Monday at 03:00
questions.task: Task: a timer that fires Mondays at 03:00. You have the unit sections but not the OnCalendar grammar. Type the page.
questions.explain: systemd.timer(5) tells you OnCalendar= exists. systemd.time(7) is where the calendar grammar, the shorthands like weekly, and the timespan units are actually defined — and it has worked examples you can copy. It is a 7 because it documents a syntax rather than a file.
questions.mnemonic: The directive is in the unit page. The grammar behind the directive is in systemd.time(7).

questions.name: the bind mount
questions.task: Task: add a bind mount to /etc/fstab. bind is not described in fstab(5). Type the page that documents it.
questions.explain: fstab(5) describes the six columns but hands the fourth one — the options — to mount(8). Every mount option you will ever need in fstab is documented under FILESYSTEM-INDEPENDENT MOUNT OPTIONS in mount(8), and filesystem-specific ones like the NFS set live in nfs(5).
questions.mnemonic: fstab(5) gives you the columns. mount(8) gives you what goes in column four.

questions.name: default ACL
questions.task: Task: set a default ACL so new files inherit it. You have forgotten the flag. Type the command to open the page, then what you press inside it to jump to the right part.
questions.explain: It is -d. The pattern here matters more than the flag: open the page, search rather than scroll, and get out. acl(5) covers the concept and the text format if you need those instead.
questions.mnemonic: Open, slash, read, q. Four moves, under fifteen seconds.

questions.name: rich rules
questions.task: Task: a firewalld rich rule that logs and rejects. Type the page with the rich rule grammar.
questions.explain: firewalld splits across a dozen pages: firewall-cmd(1) for the tool, firewalld.zone(5) for zone files, firewalld.richlanguage(5) for rich rules, firewalld.conf(5) for the daemon. man -k firewalld lists them all in one line if you cannot recall the suffix.
questions.mnemonic: One tool, many section 5 pages. When in doubt, man -k the product name.

questions.name: an nftables rule from scratch
questions.task: Task: add an nftables rule and you want a working example to copy. Type the command, then what you press inside the page.
questions.explain: nft(8) is long, and its EXAMPLES section has complete table-chain-rule blocks you can adapt. Searching straight to EXAMPLES is the single highest-value pager habit for this exam — most admin pages have one.
questions.mnemonic: Long page, unfamiliar syntax: go to EXAMPLES first, not the top.

questions.name: journalctl since yesterday
questions.task: Task: show logs from the last two hours. You are unsure what --since accepts. Type the page that defines the time expressions.
questions.explain: journalctl(1) says --since takes a timestamp and points at systemd.time(7), which is where yesterday, -1h, and the absolute formats are actually listed. Same page as the OnCalendar grammar, asked from the other direction.
questions.mnemonic: Anything systemd that smells like a date or a duration is systemd.time(7).

questions.name: nmcli, worked
questions.task: Task: create a static IPv4 connection with nmcli and you want copyable examples rather than the flag reference. Type the command.
questions.explain: NetworkManager ships a separate examples page that almost nobody finds. nmcli(1) is the flag reference, nm-settings-nmcli(5) is the property list, and nmcli-examples(7) is the one with full working command lines for static addressing, bonds and bridges.
questions.mnemonic: man -k nmcli shows all three. The examples page is the one worth opening first.
